claim: Promoter Capture Hi-C was used to generate a high-resolution atlas of chromosomal interactions involving ~22,000 gene promoters in human pluripotent and lineage-committed cells.
source: Here, we use Promoter Capture Hi-C to generate a high-resolution atlas of chromosomal interactions involving ~22,000 gene promoters in human pluripotent and lineage-committed cells, identifying putative target genes for known and predicted enhancer elements.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the use of Promoter Capture Hi-C to generate the atlas, and this is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Extensive dynamics of cis-regulatory contacts occur upon lineage commitment, including the acquisition and loss of promoter interactions.
source: We reveal extensive dynamics of cis-regulatory contacts upon lineage commitment, including the acquisition and loss of promoter interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the PCHi-C data comparing ESCs and NECs presented in the Results section.

claim: Spatial rewiring of promoter interactions occurs preferentially with predicted changes in the activity of cis-regulatory elements.
source: This spatial rewiring occurs preferentially with predicted changes in the activity of cis-regulatory elements and is associated with changes in target gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by the integration of PCHi-C data with chromatin state information and gene expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Spatial rewiring of promoter interactions is associated with changes in target gene expression.
source: This spatial rewiring occurs preferentially with predicted changes in the activity of cis-regulatory elements and is associated with changes in target gene expression.
evidence: This association is demonstrated through the integration of interaction dynamics with RNA-seq data as shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: PCHi-C identified 75,795 significant cis-interactions between promoters and other genomic regions in ESCs.
source: PCHi-C data normalisation and signal detection using the CHiCAGO pipeline (Cairns et al., 2016) identified 75,795 significant cis-interactions between promoters and other genomic regions in ESCs and 75,624 in NECs.
evidence: This is a direct result from the CHiCAGO pipeline analysis of the PCHi-C data.

claim: PCHi-C identified 75,624 significant cis-interactions between promoters and other genomic regions in NECs.
source: PCHi-C data normalisation and signal detection using the CHiCAGO pipeline (Cairns et al., 2016) identified 75,795 significant cis-interactions between promoters and other genomic regions in ESCs and 75,624 in NECs.
evidence: This is a direct result from the CHiCAGO pipeline analysis of the PCHi-C data.

claim: Approximately 300 significant trans-interactions were detected in each cell type.
source: In addition, approximately 300 significant trans-interactions were detected in each cell type.
evidence: This is reported as a result from the CHiCAGO pipeline analysis.

claim: PCHi-C samples showed an 11 to 15-fold enrichment for promoter-containing interactions over conventional Hi-C.
source: Overall, PCHi-C samples showed an 11 to 15-fold enrichment for promoter-containing interactions over conventional Hi-C.
evidence: This enrichment is calculated by comparing PCHi-C data to conventional Hi-C data generated in the same study.

claim: Promoter-interacting regions (PIRs) are significantly enriched for histone marks associated with regulatory functions in both ESCs and NECs.
source: In both cell types, promoter-interacting regions (PIRs) were significantly enriched for histone marks that are associated with regulatory functions (Figure 1C), including H3 lysine 4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), which can identify enhancers in human cell types, as well as H3 lysine four trimethylation (H3K4me3), which is associated with transcriptional activation, and H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is associated with Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Heintzman et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This enrichment is demonstrated through permutation tests comparing PIRs to distance-matched control regions, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: H3K4me1 and H3K27ac can identify enhancers in human cell types.
source: In both cell types, promoter-interacting regions (PIRs) were significantly enriched for histone marks that are associated with regulatory functions (Figure 1C), including H3 lysine 4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), which can identify enhancers in human cell types, as well as H3 lysine four trimethylation (H3K4me3), which is associated with transcriptional activation, and H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is associated with Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Heintzman et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on histone modifications.

claim: H3K4me3 is associated with transcriptional activation.
source: In both cell types, promoter-interacting regions (PIRs) were significantly enriched for histone marks that are associated with regulatory functions (Figure 1C), including H3 lysine 4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), which can identify enhancers in human cell types, as well as H3 lysine four trimethylation (H3K4me3), which is associated with transcriptional activation, and H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is associated with Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Heintzman et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on histone modifications.

claim: H3K27me3 is associated with Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression.
source: In both cell types, promoter-interacting regions (PIRs) were significantly enriched for histone marks that are associated with regulatory functions (Figure 1C), including H3 lysine 4 monomethylation (H3K4me1) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), which can identify enhancers in human cell types, as well as H3 lysine four trimethylation (H3K4me3), which is associated with transcriptional activation, and H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), which is associated with Polycomb-mediated transcriptional repression (Di Croce and Helin, 2013; Heintzman et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on histone modifications.

claim: PIRs are significantly enriched for sites bound by the architectural protein CTCF in ESCs.
source: PIRs were also significantly enriched for sites bound by the architectural protein CTCF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; based on ENCODE data available for ESCs only), consistent with previous observations in other cell types (Jin et al., 2013; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013; Sanyal et al., 2012).
evidence: This enrichment is demonstrated through permutation tests using ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq data, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type harboured either active, Polycomb-associated, or poised chromatin state signatures.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data integrated with PCHi-C data.

claim: 12,250 PIRs in ESCs harboured an active chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 7,510 PIRs in NECs harboured an active chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 3,505 PIRs in ESCs harboured a Polycomb-associated chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 5,856 PIRs in NECs harboured a Polycomb-associated chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 2,274 PIRs in ESCs harboured a poised chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 4,262 PIRs in NECs harboured a poised chromatin state signature.
source: Overall, we detected just under 20,000 PIRs in each cell type that harboured either active (12,250 in ESCs and 7510 in NECs), Polycomb-associated (3505 in ESCs and 5856 in NECs) or poised (2274 in ESCs and 4262 in NECs) chromatin state signatures, connecting a large set of putative regulatory sequences in human pluripotent and lineage committed cells to their target promoters.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis of histone modification ChIP-seq data.

claim: 25,727 PIRs in ESCs were in the background chromatin state.
source: In addition, 25,727 PIRs in ESCs and 20,016 PIRs in NECs were in the background state.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis showing no detectable signal for tested histone modifications.

claim: 20,016 PIRs in NECs were in the background chromatin state.
source: In addition, 25,727 PIRs in ESCs and 20,016 PIRs in NECs were in the background state.
evidence: This is based on ChromHMM analysis showing no detectable signal for tested histone modifications.

claim: There is significant concordance between the chromatin states at promoters and their PIRs.
source: When analysing the whole dataset, we found a significant concordance between the chromatin states at promoters and their PIRs (Figure 1D), which is in line with previous studies in other human cell types (Jin et al., 2013; Mifsud et al., 2015; Sanyal et al., 2012) and provides validation of our dataset.
evidence: This concordance is demonstrated through chi-squared tests on contingency tables as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Poised and Polycomb-associated promoters show similar interaction preferences for PIRs in either of these two states.
source: Notably, poised and Polycomb-associated promoters showed similar interaction preferences for PIRs in either of these two states (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 1D displaying log2 odds ratios for co-occurrence of chromatin states.

claim: Poised and Polycomb-associated regions are broadly interchangeable in terms of their interaction affinities, consistent with a key role for Polycomb-group proteins in mediating interactions in the poised state.
source: This finding suggests that poised and Polycomb-associated regions are broadly interchangeable in terms of their interaction affinities, which is consistent with a key role for Polycomb-group proteins in mediating interactions in the poised state (Schoenfelder et al., 2015b).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the observed interaction patterns and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Four out of five POU3F2 PIRs tested experimentally in VISTA transgenic assays showed reporter activity exclusively in neural tissues.
source: Strikingly, four out of the five POU3F2 PIRs tested experimentally in VISTA transgenic assays showed reporter activity exclusively in neural tissues, and one PIR was inactive (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on data from the VISTA Enhancer Browser showing tissue-specific reporter expression patterns.

claim: The mRNA expression pattern of mouse Pou3f2 broadly matched the combined tissue-restricted pattern of the tested human POU3F2 PIRs.
source: Furthermore, the mRNA expression pattern of mouse Pou3f2 broadly matched the combined tissue-restricted pattern of the tested human POU3F2 PIRs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This comparison is based on EMAGE gene expression database data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 219 PIRs in ESCs overlapped VISTA-annotated human elements.
source: Overall, 219 PIRs in ESCs and 267 PIRs in NECs overlapped VISTA-annotated human elements (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis between PIRs and VISTA enhancer sequences.

claim: 267 PIRs in NECs overlapped VISTA-annotated human elements.
source: Overall, 219 PIRs in ESCs and 267 PIRs in NECs overlapped VISTA-annotated human elements (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis between PIRs and VISTA enhancer sequences.

claim: NEC PIRs were strongly enriched for sequences that could drive reporter-gene activity in neural tissues and in other neuroectodermal derivatives.
source: Notably, we found that NEC PIRs were strongly enriched for sequences that could drive reporter-gene activity in neural tissues and in other neuroectodermal derivatives, such as the neural tube and cranial structures (z-score = 11, Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This enrichment is demonstrated through analysis of VISTA enhancer activity patterns as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ESC PIRs were enriched for sequences active in neural (z-score = 6.7) and non-neural tissues (z-score = 4.5) at similar levels.
source: In contrast, ESC PIRs were enriched for sequences active in neural (z-score = 6.7) and non-neural tissues (z-score = 4.5) at similar levels (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of VISTA enhancer activity patterns shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The enrichment of PIRs with neural enhancer activity in NECs relative to their enrichment in ESCs was more pronounced when focusing on PIRs in an active chromatin state.
source: Interestingly, the enrichment of PIRs with neural enhancer activity in NECs relative to their enrichment in ESCs was even more pronounced when we focused on PIRs in an active chromatin state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of VISTA enhancer activity patterns for active-state PIRs in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 267 VISTA-annotated human enhancers interact with 277 target gene promoters in NECs.
source: We detected the interactions of 267 VISTA-annotated human enhancers with 277 target gene promoters in NECs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on PCHi-C data showing interactions between VISTA enhancers and promoters.

claim: 122 PIRs (46%) interacted with their nearest gene.
source: Of these, 122 PIRs (46%) interacted with their nearest gene, which is consistent with their current annotation in the VISTA Enhancer Browser.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the distance between PIRs and their interacting promoters.

claim: Interacting promoters engage a median of four PIRs.
source: We found interacting promoters to engage a median of four PIRs (Figure 3A), consistent with findings in other human cell types (Jin et al., 2013; Sanyal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in the boxplot in Figure 3A and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: 9,008 CRUs were defined in ESCs.
source: Focusing on protein-coding genes, and considering all promoters associated with at least one PIR, we defined 9008 CRUs in ESCs and 9361 in NECs, and studied their localisation, chromatin properties and dynamics during cell lineage commitment.
evidence: This is based on the definition of CRUs as collections of PIRs connected to the same promoter.

claim: 9,361 CRUs were defined in NECs.
source: Focusing on protein-coding genes, and considering all promoters associated with at least one PIR, we defined 9008 CRUs in ESCs and 9361 in NECs, and studied their localisation, chromatin properties and dynamics during cell lineage commitment.
evidence: This is based on the definition of CRUs as collections of PIRs connected to the same promoter.

claim: CRUs spanned a median of ~230 kb in both cell types.
source: CRUs spanned a median of ~230 kb (with a range of 1 kb-200Mb) in both cell types (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the boxplot in Figure 3C.

claim: ~75% of CRUs were fully contained within a TAD in ESCs and NECs.
source: Overall, ~75% of CRUs were fully contained within a TAD in ESCs and NECs, which was significantly higher than expected by random (Figure 3D–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through permutation tests comparing observed CRU-TAD relationships to random expectations, as shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In ~25% of CRUs, either some or all PIRs localised outside of the promoter-harbouring TAD.
source: In the remaining ~25% of CRUs, either some or all PIRs localised outside of the promoter-harbouring TAD (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown through analysis of CRU-TAD relationships and examples in Figure 3H.

claim: TAD boundaries crossed by promoter interactions were generally weaker than non-crossed boundaries.
source: We found that TAD boundaries crossed by promoter interactions were generally weaker than non-crossed boundaries (Wilcoxon test p-value=1.8e-14; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical comparison of TAD boundary strength scores shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Just under 30% of CRUs were fully contained within IN boundaries.
source: For INs, we used the published genomic coordinates (available for ESCs only) that were defined on the basis of cohesin ChIA-PET and CTCF-binding data (Ji et al., 2016). Just under 30% of CRUs were fully contained within IN boundaries, and this proportion increased to ~45% when considering the largest span of each overlapping set of INs as a single unit (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU localization relative to published IN coordinates, as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: ~45% of CRUs were fully contained when considering the largest span of each overlapping set of INs as a single unit.
source: For INs, we used the published genomic coordinates (available for ESCs only) that were defined on the basis of cohesin ChIA-PET and CTCF-binding data (Ji et al., 2016). Just under 30% of CRUs were fully contained within IN boundaries, and this proportion increased to ~45% when considering the largest span of each overlapping set of INs as a single unit (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU localization relative to published IN coordinates, as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CRUs are partially constrained by, but not fully contained within, higher order topological structures such as TADs and INs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CRUs are partially constrained by, but not fully contained within, higher order topological structures such as TADs and INs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that while CRUs show preferential localization within TADs and INs, a substantial fraction extend beyond these boundaries.

claim: 18% of CRUs in ESCs contained combinations of PIRs in active, poised and Polycomb-associated chromatin states.
source: In contrast to these 'uniform' CRUs, 18% of CRUs in ESCs and 24% in NECs contained combinations of PIRs in active, poised and Polycomb-associated chromatin states (clusters 4–7; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering of CRUs according to their PIR chromatin state distributions, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 24% of CRUs in NECs contained combinations of PIRs in active, poised and Polycomb-associated chromatin states.
source: In contrast to these 'uniform' CRUs, 18% of CRUs in ESCs and 24% in NECs contained combinations of PIRs in active, poised and Polycomb-associated chromatin states (clusters 4–7; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering of CRUs according to their PIR chromatin state distributions, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The chromatin state of each promoter generally matched that of the most prevalent CRU chromatin state.
source: Notably, the chromatin state of each promoter generally matched that of the most prevalent CRU chromatin state (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmaps displaying log2 odds ratios of promoter states associated with each CRU cluster in Figure 4A.

claim: 65% of the single-state CRUs in ESCs remained single-state CRUs in NECs.
source: We found that 65% of the single-state CRUs in ESCs remained single-state CRUs in NECs, although approximately half of them switched their state (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU state transitions between ESCs and NECs, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Approximately half of the single-state CRUs that remained single-state switched their state upon ESC to NEC differentiation.
source: We found that 65% of the single-state CRUs in ESCs remained single-state CRUs in NECs, although approximately half of them switched their state (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU state transitions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 11% of CRUs lost a dual-state configuration on ESC to NEC differentiation.
source: In addition, similar proportions of CRUs lost (11%) and acquired (13%) a dual-state configuration on ESC to NEC differentiation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU state transitions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 13% of CRUs acquired a dual-state configuration on ESC to NEC differentiation.
source: In addition, similar proportions of CRUs lost (11%) and acquired (13%) a dual-state configuration on ESC to NEC differentiation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CRU state transitions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CRU state transitions associated significantly with changes in the expression of their target genes.
source: CRU state transitions associated significantly with changes in the expression of their target genes (p-value<0.005, Fisher's exact test; Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This association is demonstrated through Fisher's exact tests on contingency tables shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Genes that were transcriptionally upregulated upon ESC differentiation preferentially gained an active single-state in NECs.
source: In particular, genes that were transcriptionally upregulated upon ESC differentiation preferentially gained an active single-state in NECs, either through switching the chromatin state of a single-state CRU (Figure 5B) or through resolving a dual-state CRU (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown through the heatmaps in Figure 5B,C displaying log2 odds ratios for CRU state transitions and gene expression changes.

claim: 1,153 rewired interactions (present in only one cell type) were identified at high confidence.
source: To distinguish between interactions that are rewired and retained on ESC differentiation at high confidence, we applied additional filters to the PCHi-C data, resulting in 1153 rewired (present in only one cell type) and 1258 retained (present in both ESCs and NECs) interactions (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on stringent filtering criteria applied to PCHi-C data to identify high-confidence interaction dynamics.

claim: 1,258 retained interactions (present in both ESCs and NECs) were identified at high confidence.
source: To distinguish between interactions that are rewired and retained on ESC differentiation at high confidence, we applied additional filters to the PCHi-C data, resulting in 1153 rewired (present in only one cell type) and 1258 retained (present in both ESCs and NECs) interactions (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on stringent filtering criteria applied to PCHi-C data to identify high-confidence interaction dynamics.

claim: The co-occurrence of rewiring and recolouring interactions on ESC differentiation was significantly more common than expected at random.
source: Importantly, we found that the co-occurrence of rewiring and recolouring interactions on ESC differentiation was significantly more common than expected at random (Figure 6B, p-value<0.001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Fisher's exact test on the contingency table shown in Figure 6B.

claim: New interactions that were gained by NECs preferentially acquired the active state, or transitioned from the background to repressed state.
source: Specifically, new interactions that were gained by NECs preferentially acquired the active state, or transitioned from the background to repressed state (Figure 6B, bottom row).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 6B displaying associations between PIR chromatin state transitions and interaction dynamics.

claim: Interactions that were lost on ESC differentiation were enriched for PIRs that transitioned from the active to poised/Polycomb-associated states, as well as for those switching to the background state.
source: Interactions that were lost on ESC differentiation were enriched for PIRs that transitioned from the active to poised/Polycomb-associated states, as well as for those switching to the background state (Figure 6B, middle row).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 6B displaying associations between PIR chromatin state transitions and interaction dynamics.

claim: 99.7% of rewiring events were not associated with larger-scale A/B compartment dynamics.
source: Notably, the vast majority of rewiring events (99.7%) were not associated with larger-scale A/B compartment dynamics (not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of rewiring events in the context of A/B compartment changes.

claim: 25% of PIRs that were retained in both cell types undergo chromatin state recolouring.
source: Finally, we observed that 25% of PIRs that were retained in both cell types undergo chromatin state recolouring (Figure 6E, red segment).
evidence: This is shown in the pie chart in Figure 6E summarizing retained interaction scenarios.

claim: The loss or gain of interactions with active-state PIRs associated significantly with changes in gene expression.
source: We found that the loss or gain of interactions with active-state PIRs associated significantly with changes in gene expression (Figure 6G), suggesting their functional contribution to transcriptional control.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Wilcoxon rank sum tests comparing gene expression changes for different PIR dynamics scenarios, as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Gene expression changes were detected at retained and recoloured PIRs.
source: Notably, gene expression changes were detected at retained and recoloured PIRs (Figure 6G, left panel), and also when active-state PIRs were lost or gained through rewiring (Figure 6G, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in the boxplots in Figure 6G comparing gene expression changes for recolouring and rewiring scenarios.

claim: Gene expression changes were detected when active-state PIRs were lost or gained through rewiring.
source: Notably, gene expression changes were detected at retained and recoloured PIRs (Figure 6G, left panel), and also when active-state PIRs were lost or gained through rewiring (Figure 6G, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in the boxplots in Figure 6G comparing gene expression changes for recolouring and rewiring scenarios.

claim: Chromatin state changes and rewiring of interactions at PIRs contribute jointly to transcriptional regulation.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that chromatin state changes and rewiring of interactions at PIRs contribute jointly to transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed associations between both recolouring and rewiring events with gene expression changes.

claim: Promoter interaction dynamics preferentially co-occur with chromatin state dynamics upon cell lineage commitment.
source: Furthermore, our results show that promoter interaction dynamics preferentially co-occur with chromatin state dynamics upon cell lineage commitment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the significant co-occurrence of rewiring and recolouring events shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cell fate decisions are associated with profound changes in chromatin organisation.
source: Cell fate decisions are associated with profound changes in chromatin organisation, which underlie the activation of lineage-specific and the silencing of lineage-inappropriate genes (Buecker and Wysocka, 2012; Bulger and Groudine, 2010; Calo and Wysocka, 2013; Hallikas et al., 2006; Ong and Corces, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Cis-regulatory elements such as transcriptional enhancers play a key role in cell fate decisions by integrating regulatory inputs from intrinsic and extracellular cues.
source: Cis-regulatory elements such as transcriptional enhancers play a key role in this process by integrating regulatory inputs from intrinsic and extracellular cues, and by mediating the recruitment of core activator and repressor complexes (Pennacchio et al., 2013; Shlyueva et al., 2014; Spitz and Furlong, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on enhancer function.

claim: Cis-regulatory elements are often considerable distances away from their target gene promoters and may not control their nearest genes.
source: Cis-regulatory elements are often considerable distances away from their target gene promoters and may not control their nearest genes (Carvajal et al., 2001; Jeong et al., 2006; Marinić et al., 2013; Pennacchio et al., 2006; Ruf et al., 2011; Sagai et al., 2005; Spitz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating long-range enhancer-promoter interactions.

claim: Long-range action of cis-regulatory elements is facilitated by DNA-looping interactions.
source: It is generally accepted that this long-range action is facilitated by DNA-looping interactions (Pennacchio et al., 2013; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on enhancer-promoter interactions.

claim: The target genes of most cis-regulatory elements remain unknown.
source: As a result, the target genes of most cis-regulatory elements remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of challenges in predicting regulatory interactions from sequence and epigenetic information.

claim: Many genes are controlled by multiple regulatory elements.
source: Furthermore, while it is generally accepted that many genes are controlled by multiple regulatory elements (Barolo, 2012; Miguel-Escalada et al., 2015) our understanding of multi-modular gene regulation remains limited, particularly in the context of mammalian development and stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on multi-enhancer gene regulation.

claim: NECs were generated using an established protocol.
source: We generated NECs using an established protocol (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and confirmed efficient differentiation by flow cytometry analysis and RNA-sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on the use of a published differentiation protocol and validation through multiple assays.

claim: Efficient differentiation of ESCs to NECs was confirmed by flow cytometry analysis and RNA-sequencing.
source: We generated NECs using an established protocol (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and confirmed efficient differentiation by flow cytometry analysis and RNA-sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry data showing lineage marker expression and RNA-seq data showing appropriate gene expression changes, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Raw sequencing reads have been deposited to Gene Expression Omnibus (accession GSE86821).
source: Processed datasets have been made available through Open Science Framework (http://osf.io/sdbg4), and raw sequencing reads have been deposited to Gene Expression Omnibus (accession GSE86821).
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: Processed datasets have been made available through Open Science Framework.
source: Processed datasets have been made available through Open Science Framework (http://osf.io/sdbg4), and raw sequencing reads have been deposited to Gene Expression Omnibus (accession GSE86821).
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.
